section_1.title: The Flatlander’s Dilemma (0:00-0:45)
section_1.content: Introduce the concept of 'Dimensional Limitation.' Use the analogy of a 2D square living on a piece of paper who cannot perceive a 3D sphere passing through its world, only a circle that expands and shrinks. Prerequisite: Understanding coordinates (x, y).
section_1.example: A 2D ant crawling on a sheet of paper. When a ball touches the paper, the ant only sees a growing and shrinking circular shadow.

section_2.title: The Logic of Dimensional Projection (0:45-2:00)
section_2.content: Define 'Projection' as the reduction of dimension. Explain how a 3D object casts a 2D shadow, and a 4D object (tesseract) would cast a 3D shadow. Use grid-based visualizations to show vertices shifting.
section_2.example: A wireframe cube casting a shadow on a wall. By rotating the cube, the shadow changes shape—this represents the 'shift' in perspective across dimensions.

section_3.title: The Geometry of the Tesseract (2:00-3:30)
section_3.content: Introduce the Hypercube (Tesseract). Explain the rule: A 0D point moves to create a 1D line; a 1D line moves to create a 2D square; a 2D square moves to create a 3D cube; a 3D cube moves into the '4th direction' (W-axis) to create a Tesseract.
section_3.example: An animation showing a small cube inside a large cube, with connecting lines (extrusions) appearing to stretch and contract as it 'rotates' through 4D space.

section_4.title: Solving the Shift: The Unfolding Puzzle (3:30-4:30)
section_4.content: Apply the concept to a puzzle: How to 'unfold' a 4D tesseract into a 3D cross (the Dalí Cross). Focus on the concept of 'nets' (similar to unfolding a 3D box into a 2D cross pattern).
section_4.example: The 'Dali Cross'—showing how 8 cubes can be unfolded into a 3D shape, just like a 6-sided die unfolds into a flat paper cross.

section_5.title: Conclusion and Intuition Check (4:30-5:00)
section_5.content: Summarize that dimensional shifts are about tracking how geometry 'bleeds' from one dimension to another. Emphasize that we perceive 4D objects through their 3D 'slices'.
section_5.example: A device (like an MRI scanner) taking 2D slices of a 3D apple; if we were 2D beings, we would 'reconstruct' the apple by seeing these slices appear sequentially.
